title: Project & Agile Delivery Management
subtitle: Initiate, plan, run and close projects — with classic project management and agile delivery.
outcomes: Explain the project life cycle and the project manager's role
Plan scope, schedule, budget and risk
Run agile delivery with Scrum, user stories and roadmaps
Report progress and close a project well

pool.q: How does the purpose of operations differ from the purpose of a project?
options: Operations keep the organisation running; a project meets its goals and ends
pool.explain: Projects are temporary and unique; operations are ongoing and repetitive.
pool.evidence: The purpose of operations is to keep the organization functioning while the purpose of a project is to meet its goals and conclude.

pool.q: Is assembling cars on a production line a project?
options: Yes, every car is a project
Only if it takes more than a year
No — it is an operation, a repetitive process
pool.explain: Designing a new car model, by contrast, would be a project.
pool.evidence: the actual assembly of the cars is considered an operation (i.e., a repetitive process that is followed for most makes and models)

pool.q: What does project management include?
options: Planning, putting the plan into action, and measuring progress and performance
pool.explain: Planning, executing and monitoring repeat throughout the project.
pool.evidence: Project management is a process that includes planning, putting the project plan into action, and measuring progress and performance.

pool.q: Which project environment factors are most often misunderstood or ignored?
pool.explain: Physical factors are the easiest to understand.
pool.evidence: it is the cultural and international factors that are often misunderstood or ignored

pool.q: What must project staff know about their work?
options: What is expected, when, and the budget, time and quality constraints
pool.explain: Clear expectations prevent wasted effort.
pool.evidence: It is essential that your project staff know what is expected of them

pool.q: In the project life cycle, which two questions do feasibility and justification answer?
options: Can we do the project? Should we do the project?
When does it end? How long will it take?
pool.explain: A feasibility study compares options before a project is initiated.
pool.evidence: Issues of feasibility (“can we do the project?”) and justification (“should we do the project?”) are addressed.

pool.q: Who decides whether a project is worth undertaking and will be profitable for the organisation?
pool.explain: The sponsor owns the business case.
pool.evidence: It is up to the project sponsor to determine if the project is worth undertaking and whether the project will be profitable to the organization.

pool.q: What happens in the project initiation phase?
options: The problem is identified, a solution defined, a project formed and a team appointed
The project is closed and archived
pool.explain: Initiation is the first phase of the project life cycle.
pool.evidence: Within the initiation phase, the business problem or opportunity is identified, a solution is defined, a project is formed, and a project team is appointed

pool.q: Who should set project objectives so they are achievable and realistic?
options: Managers jointly with the people who do the work
pool.explain: Those doing the work know what is realistic.
pool.evidence: they must be determined jointly by managers and those who perform the work

pool.q: How is a project's return on investment (ROI) calculated?
options: Benefits divided by the number of team members
Benefits minus costs, divided by costs
Total costs divided by the project's duration
pool.explain: ROI expresses the net gain relative to what was invested.
pool.evidence: This is calculated by subtracting the project’s costs from the benefits and then dividing by the costs.

pool.q: What are project deliverables?
options: Tangible outcomes, measurable results or specific items that must be produced to complete the project or phase
pool.explain: Describe each deliverable in enough detail to tell it apart from related ones.
pool.evidence: Project deliverables are tangible outcomes, measurable results, or specific items that must be produced to consider either the project or the project phase completed.

pool.q: How detailed must project deliverables be described?
options: Enough to tell them apart from related deliverables
pool.explain: Clear descriptions avoid disputes about what was promised.
pool.evidence: All deliverables must be described in a sufficient level of detail so that they can be differentiated from related deliverables.

pool.q: What do a project's requirements describe?
options: What the project should accomplish and how it should be created and implemented
pool.explain: Requirements are defined in the scope plan.
pool.evidence: describe what a project is supposed to accomplish and how the project is supposed to be created and implemented

pool.q: How does a requirements traceability matrix help?
options: It assigns tasks to team members
It links each requirement to business and project objectives so it adds business value
pool.explain: It also tracks requirements through the life cycle so approved ones are delivered.
pool.evidence: The implementation of a requirements traceability matrix helps ensure that each requirement adds business value by linking it to the business and project objectives.

pool.q: Why is a dependency called 'finish-to-start'?
options: Because the first activity's finish leads into the second activity's start
Because the project starts when it finishes
Because the second task must finish first
pool.explain: It is the most common dependency type in network diagrams.
pool.evidence: It’s called finish-to-start because the first activity’s finish leads into the second activity’s start

pool.q: Why are Gantt charts commonly used?
options: They are easy to read and show schedule activities
pool.explain: Bars show each activity's start, end and duration.
pool.evidence: Gantt charts are easy to read and are commonly used to display schedule activities.

pool.q: Managing a project in an unfamiliar field, how can you define its tasks?
options: Guess from past projects in other fields
Bring in experts in that field to help
pool.explain: Experts help you understand what activities are involved.
pool.evidence: you might also use experts in that particular field to help define tasks

pool.q: Which tasks must be included in a network diagram?
options: Only the first and last tasks
All the tasks in the work breakdown structure
pool.explain: Every WBS task has to be accounted for in the schedule.
pool.evidence: All of the WBS tasks must be included in the network because they have to be accounted for in the schedule.

pool.q: What is a limitation of the activity-on-arrow (AOA) method?
options: It can only show finish-to-start relationships
It only works for one-day projects
pool.explain: Activity-on-node diagrams are more flexible.
pool.evidence: The AOA network can only show finish-to-start relationships.

pool.q: Do dummy activities in a network diagram have durations?
pool.explain: They only show dependencies between tasks.
pool.evidence: Dummy activities do not have durations associated with them.

pool.q: What is a parametric estimate?
options: Using average costs per unit for activities common to many projects
pool.explain: For example, estimating truck size from the number of bedrooms in a move.
pool.evidence: If the project consists of activities that are common to many other projects, average costs are available per unit.

pool.q: How much time and resources should go into making estimates?
options: An amount appropriate to the project's size and complexity
pool.explain: Estimates must be accurate enough to be meaningful, but not cost more than they're worth.
pool.evidence: the amount of time and resources used to make the estimates should be appropriate to the size and complexity of the project

pool.q: In earned value management, what is the planned value (PV)?
options: The value of the work actually completed
The amount of work that should have been done by a particular date
The budget left at the end
pool.explain: Comparing PV, earned value and actual cost shows schedule and cost performance.
pool.evidence: The amount of work that should have been done by a particular date is the planned value (PV)

pool.q: For which projects is earned value management (EVM) widely used?
pool.explain: EVM compares planned value, earned value and actual cost.
pool.evidence: A method that is widely used for medium- and high-complexity projects is the earned value management (EVM) method.

pool.q: When is accepting a risk your only choice?
options: When the risk is very likely
When you can't avoid it and nothing can reduce its impact
pool.explain: Other responses are to avoid, mitigate or transfer the risk.
pool.evidence: If you can’t avoid the risk, and there’s nothing you can do to reduce its impact, then accepting it is your only choice.

pool.q: What is a common risk avoidance technique?
options: Using proven, existing technologies instead of new ones
pool.explain: New techniques may promise more but carry more risk.
pool.evidence: A common risk avoidance technique is to use proven and existing technologies rather than adopt new techniques

pool.q: How is contingency typically managed in a project budget?
pool.explain: Its size depends on the risks identified.
pool.evidence: contingency is typically managed as one line item in the project budget

pool.q: Which events are outside the project team's control?
options: Weather, political unrest and labour strikes
pool.explain: Such risks may only be accepted or mitigated, not avoided.
pool.evidence: Weather, political unrest, and labour strikes are examples of events that can significantly impact the project and that are outside the control of the project team.

pool.q: What is Kanban?
options: A way of visualising and improving current working practices so work flows quickly
pool.explain: Smooth flow delivers value quickly and gets early feedback.
pool.evidence: Kanban is a way of visualising and improving your current working practices so that work flows through a system quickly.

pool.q: Whose needs must agile teams prioritise, even above senior stakeholders'?
pool.explain: Agile is about constantly putting users first.
pool.evidence: including those of your senior stakeholders

pool.q: After building something that meets the most important user need, what should you do?
options: Show it to users, listen to their feedback and improve it
Launch it and never change it
pool.explain: Then repeat for the next most important need.
pool.evidence: Show it to your users, listen to their feedback and improve it.

pool.q: Which of these is one of the core principles of agile delivery?
options: Plan everything once at the start
pool.explain: Others include focusing on user needs and delivering iteratively.
pool.evidence: fail fast and learn quickly

pool.q: How does the Scrum Guide define Scrum?
options: A lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems
A detailed method that prescribes every task
pool.explain: Scrum is deliberately incomplete, defining only what is required.
pool.evidence: Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems.

pool.q: How long is the Sprint Review timeboxed for a one-month Sprint?
pool.explain: Shorter Sprints have shorter reviews.
pool.evidence: is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint

pool.q: Should a Sprint Review be just a presentation?
options: No — it is a working session
Yes, by the Product Owner only
pool.explain: Stakeholders and the team discuss progress toward the Product Goal.
pool.evidence: The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.

pool.q: What is the most important part of a user story?
pool.explain: Stories briefly explain the actor, the narrative and — most importantly — the goal.
pool.evidence: The most important part of a user story is the goal.

pool.q: How often should prioritisation decisions be made?
options: Regularly — e.g. weekly for the sprint backlog and quarterly for the roadmap
Once at the start of the project
pool.explain: Priorities change as you learn more.
pool.evidence: weekly to prioritise the sprint backlog, or quarterly to organise the service roadmap

pool.q: What should prioritisation decisions be based on?
options: The loudest opinion in the room
Performance analysis, user research and stakeholder input
pool.explain: Use a clear prioritisation method and involve the team.
pool.evidence: They should be based on performance analysis, user research and input from stakeholders.

pool.q: What is a roadmap?
options: A plan showing how a product or service is likely to develop over time
pool.explain: It makes clear the goal and the steps toward it.
pool.evidence: A roadmap is a plan that shows how a product or service is likely to develop over time.

pool.q: Who usually leads creating and updating a roadmap?
pool.explain: The team and stakeholders should be involved too.
pool.evidence: Creating and iterating a roadmap is something you do collaboratively, usually led by your product manager.

pool.q: Who should be able to see your agile planning?
options: Anyone in your organisation, through online tools
pool.explain: Openness builds shared understanding.
pool.evidence: You should also allow anyone in your organisation to see any planning you do using online tools.

pool.q: If you have a fixed deadline, how should you focus roadmap planning?
options: On everything you would like to build
On what you can achieve within that deadline
pool.explain: Fixed deadlines, such as ministerial ones, constrain scope.
pool.evidence: you should focus your roadmap planning around what you can achieve within that deadline

pool.q: Besides defining objectives, what should a team have?
options: A rule never to change objectives
A system for checking when objectives are achieved
A separate team for each objective
pool.explain: Measurable objectives show real progress.
pool.evidence: have a system for checking when you

pool.q: What is a punch list?
options: A list of minor items still to be repaired or completed before closing
pool.explain: Clearing it is part of closing the contract.
pool.evidence: any minor items that need to be repaired or completed are placed on a punch list

pool.q: What should project information gathered during completion reflect?
options: The characteristics and specifications of the final product
pool.explain: Documentation should match what was actually delivered.
pool.evidence: The project information you are collecting during this phase should reflect the characteristics and specifications of the final product.

pool.q: If you administer a contract yourself, whom should you ask about special conditions?
pool.explain: Missing a condition can delay project closure.
pool.evidence: be sure to ask your procurement department if there are any special conditions

pool.q: What is a lessons-learned meeting?
options: A review before the team disbands to capture what the project taught
pool.explain: Some organisations feed lessons into their work processes.
pool.evidence: a review is conducted to capture the lessons that can be learned from this project, often called a lessons-learned meeting or document

pool.q: If estimates often differ from actual costs, what should be reviewed?
pool.explain: Better methods improve future estimates.
pool.evidence: If the estimates are frequently different from the actual costs, the choice of estimating method is reviewed.
